en: Oṃ, salutation to Śiva!
This is the series of verses for the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, which is free from the constraints imposed by destiny, consists solely of bliss, and is not dependent on anything else.
Victorious is the speech of the poet, which brings forth a creation that delights in the nine aesthetic flavors (rasas).
Poetry leads to fame, the accomplishment of wealth, proficiency in worldly conduct,
the warding off of misfortune, immediate supreme bliss, and, by being equal to a beloved mistress, it is conducive to instruction.
Genius, proficiency gained from the study of the world, the sciences, and poetry, and practice under the instruction of those who know poetry—these are the causes for its arising. (MK 3)

When word and meaning are free from defects, endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇas*), and sometimes even without ornaments (*alaṃkāras*), this is the highest [type of poetry]; when the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) excels the expressed (*vācya*), it is called *dhvani* by the wise. (MKpr-K_4)
When the suggested meaning is subordinate, it is called *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), which is considered mediocre;
when there is no suggested meaning, it is *śabdacitra* (verbal artistry) or *vācyacitra* (conceptual artistry), which is remembered as inferior.
In this context, a word may be of three kinds: denotative (*vācaka*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), or suggestive (*vyañjaka*).
Its meanings may be the denoted (*vācya*) and so forth; furthermore, for some, there is also the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
It is generally accepted that all words possess the capacity to suggest meanings as well. That word which directly expresses the meaning conventionally assigned to it is called a "denoter" (vācaka).
The conventional [meaning] is fourfold—consisting of genus (*jāti*) and so forth—or it is genus alone;
that is the primary meaning, and the primary function toward it is called "denotation" (*abhidhā*).

When the primary meaning is sublated, yet there is a connection [between that meaning and another], and another meaning is indicated either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*), that is *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which is a superimposed operation.
The throwing of one’s own [meaning] to another for its own establishment, and the surrendering of one’s own [meaning] to another for its own purpose;
it is said that this pure [metaphor] is of two kinds: appropriation (*upādāna*) and indication (*lakṣaṇa*).
But another is *sāropā* (superimposition), where both the object and the subject are mentioned;
that in which the object is included within the subject would be *sādhyavasānikā* (identification).

These two types of secondary [metaphorical] usage are to be understood as being based on similarity or another type of relationship; they are further divided into the figurative and the pure. Therefore, indication (lakṣaṇā) is of six kinds.
When devoid of a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), it is conventional (rūḍhi); when accompanied by one, it serves a specific purpose (prayojana).
And that [purpose] may be either hidden (gūḍha) or manifest (agūḍha); thus, this [metaphor] is said to be of three kinds.
The operation consisting of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) has that [indication] as its basis;
it is employed there in order to bring about the cognition of that [suggested meaning] for which indication is resorted to.
In this case, where the fruit is cognizable solely through words, there is no function other than suggestion (*vyañjanā*);
there is no denotation (*abhidhā*) because of the absence of convention (*samaya*), nor is there indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the absence of a cause.
Here, there is neither a primary object of reference nor any sublation; there is no connection with a result, nor is there any purpose in this, nor does the word falter in its meaning. (MK 16)
In this way, there would be an infinite regress that destroys the very root;
it is not tenable that the object to be characterized should be accompanied by its purpose.
For it has been stated that the object of knowledge is one thing and its fruit is another;
there is no such indication by secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for the qualified [object], as the qualifiers would instead be indicated by the indicated [object].

When the denotative capacity of a word with multiple meanings has been restricted by means such as association (saṃyoga) and so forth, the activity that produces a cognition of a meaning not [explicitly] denoted is "coloration" (añjana).

The word, when conjoined with that [meaning], is the manifester; likewise, the meaning, when conjoined with another meaning, is also considered a manifester therein by virtue of being a cooperative cause.
The meanings have been explained previously; now, their capacity to manifest [those meanings] is being described:
[it arises] from the speaker, the person to be addressed, the intonation (*kāku*), the sentence, the expressed meaning, and the proximity of other factors.
For those endowed with creative intuition (*pratibhā*), that operation which— due to the particularity of the introductory context, place, time, and so forth—
causes the cognition of one meaning from a [given] meaning is indeed manifestation (*vyakti*).
Since an object known through the means of valid cognition of verbal testimony manifests another object,
the word serves as a cooperative cause for that manifestation of the object.
In that [type of] dhvani where the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary,
the expressed meaning is either transferred into another meaning or completely set aside.
Where the intended meaning is subordinate to another, that is the other [type of suggestion];
moreover, there is that in which the sequence of the suggested is unperceived, and the other in which the sequence of the suggested is perceived.
The aesthetic flavor (rasa), the emotion (bhāva), the semblance thereof (tadābhāsa), the cessation of emotion (bhāvaśānti), and so forth, exist as a non-sequential [process];
they are distinct from the ornaments of rasa and the like, standing as that which is to be ornamented.
If those causes, effects,
and auxiliary factors that exist in the world for a stable emotion such as love are likewise present in drama and poetry, [then how can there be a distinction between them]?
Those which have become manifest and those which have not yet become manifest are called the transitory states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
That stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), when made manifest by those factors such as the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, is known as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

In drama, eight aesthetic sentiments (rasas) are traditionally taught: the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the odious, and that which is called the marvelous.
Love, mirth, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder— these are proclaimed as the stable emotional states (sthāyibhāvas).
Disgust, lassitude, apprehension, as well as envy, intoxication, fatigue, indolence, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, and fortitude; MK 31.
Shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, as well as dullness, pride, despondency, longing, sleep, and epilepsy. (MK 32)
Sleep, awakening, indignation, dissimulation, and then ferocity; mental confusion, disease, madness, and likewise even death.
Terror and deliberation are also to be known as transitory mental states;
these thirty-three states have thus been fully enumerated by name.
There is also the ninth rasa, the Tranquil (śānta), which has detachment (nirveda) as its dominant emotion;
likewise, love directed toward gods and other such objects, when manifested as a transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva), constitutes it.

Emotion (bhāva) has been described; those which appear as such but are prompted by impropriety are its semblances (tadābhāsa). Furthermore, there is the subsidence (śānti), the emergence (udaya), the conjunction (sandhi), and the mingling (śabalatā) of emotion.
Even when they occur within the primary rasa, they occasionally attain the status of being subordinate;
however, this applies only to that which exists as a suggested meaning whose sequence is imperceptible, resembling a resonance (anusvāna).
That *dhvani* is said to be threefold, arising from the power of the word, the meaning, or both;
therein, either an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) or a fact (*vastu*) itself is manifested through the word and so forth.
That [suggestion] arising from the power of the word (śabdaśaktyudbhava) is to be known as twofold by virtue of its predominance;
likewise, the meaning (artha) arising from the power of the meaning (arthaśaktyudbhava) that functions as a suggester is possible both inherently (svataḥ) and [through external factors].
Whether established through mere bold assertion (prauḍhokti) by the poet or by his creation,
and whether it be a fact (vastu) or an ornament (alaṅkāra)— this [suggestion], which has six such varieties, reveals that which [is intended].
Alternatively, it may be either a matter of substance (vastu) or an ornament (alaṅkāra); thus, this [poetry] consists of twelve types.
Since one type arises from both word and meaning, its divisions consequently amount to eighteen.
Because aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and the like are infinite, they are counted as a single category.

Suggestion arising from the sentence occurs in the sentence; others hold it occurs even in a word; and that which arises from the power of the meaning occurs even in a literary composition (*prabandha*).
Even within the syllables that constitute a portion of a word, there are aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and other elements;
these fifty-one varieties, when combined with one another, [yield further distinctions].
By means of the threefold confusion and the single-fold commixture, [the numbers are] four, zero, four, and zero;
five, five, two, and one.

The "limb" (aṅga) of another [poetic figure] that is not concealed is the "limb for the accomplishment of the expressed" (vācyasiddhyaṅga); [the figures] "obvious," "doubtful," "of equal prominence," "suggested by intonation" (kākākṣipta), and "unpleasant" [are also varieties].
Thus, eight varieties of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) have been recorded;
their further subdivisions should be understood as before, according to their respective applications.

Through their connection with those [other] figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*), as well as through combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) and commingling (*saṃkara*), the number of varieties of *dhvani* becomes exceedingly vast due to these mutual combinations.

Regarding the two types of poetry previously illustrated as "wondrous in word" and "wondrous in meaning," therein the two— wondrous meaning and wondrous word— exist according to the predominance of the poetic qualities (guṇa).
The impairment of the primary meaning is a defect, and the aesthetic flavor (rasa) is the primary [meaning] because it is based upon that expressed meaning.
Since words and other elements are useful for both, that [defect] applies to them as well.

A faulty word is one that is harsh to the ear, grammatically incorrect, unidiomatic, or semantically powerless; it may have its meaning obscured, convey an inappropriate sense, be redundant, fail to express the intended meaning, or be indecent in three ways.
That which is ambiguous, unintelligible, vulgar, of indirect meaning, or moreover, corrupted;
that whose predicate portion is not clearly distinguished, or which causes a contradiction—these faults reside only within the compound.
Setting aside [the defects] of corrupted formation, incapacity, and meaninglessness, these same defects exist in a sentence as well; some of them also occur in a portion of a word.

[The defects are: disagreeable color, damaged or omitted *visarga*, lack of euphonic conjunction (*visandhi*), ruined meter, deficient or redundant words, repeated words, falling excellence, and resuming what has already been concluded.
A compound with only one word for two meanings, non-connection of intended meanings, the unstated expressed meaning,
a compound with a word placed in the wrong position, the confused, the parenthetical, and that which contradicts common usage.

Likewise, a sentence may have a broken sequence, lack of sequence, or be devoid of self-interest and interest for others; it may be deficient in meaning, harsh, contradictory, repetitive, poorly ordered, or vulgar.

The uncertain, the reasonless, the contradicted by common knowledge and by science, the unqualified, and those involving the reversal of specificities regarding restriction and non-restriction; these are the [fallacies]. (MKV 56)

[The fallacies are: that which is accompanied by an expectation [of further qualification], that which is joined with a subordinate term (*upapada*), that which is distinct from its usual companion (*sahacara*), that which expresses a contradiction, that which is improperly combined as a prescription or a restatement, that which involves a relinquished [position] and a re-adopted one, and that which is indecorous (*aślīla*).

In expressions such as *karṇāvataṃsa* ("ear-ornament"), the employment of words like "ear" (*karṇa*) is for the purpose of conveying proximity and so forth; this justification applies to cases where [the parts] are already established.
When the meaning is well-known, a lack of reason is not a fault; however, in the case of imitation, it is so for all [styles].
Due to the propriety of the speaker and other factors, even a defect may sometimes become a merit, and sometimes neither.

The verbal expression of transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva), aesthetic flavors (rasa), and stable emotions (sthāyibhāva), as well as the manifestation of the ensuants (anubhāva) and the determinants (vibhāva) through laborious conceptualization; [these constitute defects].
The apprehension of discordant excitants and so forth, excessive intensity, repetition,
abrupt expansion and interruption, and even the over-elaboration of subordinate elements.
The failure to maintain the connection with the dominant emotion (aṅgin), the inversion of the constituent factors (prakṛti),
and the mention of what is not a constituent factor— such are the defects in a rasa.
There is no fault even when a transitory emotion (saṃcārībhāva) is expressed by its own name in certain cases;
indeed, the expression of a conflicting or sublated transitory emotion and the like is conducive to poetic merit.
That which is contradictory when residing in the same substratum must be made to reside in a different substratum;
likewise, a sentiment that is [contradictory] in immediate succession must be separated by another sentiment.
Even if two [elements] are contradictory when being recollected, if they are intended to be equal,
or if both attain the status of being subordinate to a primary subject (aṅgin), they are not mutually defective.
Those properties of the aesthetic flavor (rasa), which are like the qualities of bravery and so forth belonging to the self,
and which serve as causes for its excellence while remaining fixed, are called *guṇas*.
Those things such as the "Theft" (stena) and "Fortress" (prāsa), like necklaces and other ornaments, sometimes assist that [entity] which is real by means of their constituent parts.
These qualities are three—known as sweetness (*mādhurya*), vigor (*ojas*), and clarity (*prasāda*)—and not ten.
Sweetness consists in the quality of being delightful; it is the cause of melting (*druti*) in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).

Ojas, which is characterized by an excellence of light due to the expansion of the self, resides in the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) and serves as the cause for its manifestation in compassion, separation, and the tranquility thereof.

In the *bībhatsa* (disgust) and *raudra* (fury) sentiments, there is a gradual increase of that [feeling], like fire on dry fuel; whereas in the case of one who is like clear water, it occurs all at once.
This clarity pervades the other [element], its presence established everywhere;
moreover, it is held that the function of those [guṇas] toward word and meaning occurs through the operation of the guṇas.
Some are included within these [categories], others resort to the abandonment of faults;
still others assume the state of being a fault in some respect—therefore, there are not ten [types of persons].
Therefore, neither the qualities of meaning nor those qualities of sound that have been mentioned need to be stated;
rather, phonemes, compounds, and stylistic arrangement are said to be their manifestors.
In [the quality of] sweetness (*mādhurya*), the stops (*sparśa*) ending in the last letter of each class [of consonants], excluding the *ṭa*-class, as well as *ra* and *ṇa*, are light;
likewise, the arrangement [of words] involves repetition or a middling cadence (*madhyavṛtti*).
In the *ojas* [style], there is the *yoga* (conjunction) of the first and third letters with the last two, the substitution of *ra* for similar letters,
the *ṭa*-class consonants, *śa* and *ṣa*, alliteration, protracted vowels, and a forceful composition.
That quality by which the comprehension of meaning occurs from a word through mere hearing is considered the common grace (prasāda) shared by all [the causes].
In certain instances, due to the propriety of the speaker, the subject matter, and the composition,
a variation in the arrangement, the meter, and the phonemes is also accepted.
When a statement is spoken in one way but is interpreted by another in a different way—
either through punning (*śleṣa*) or through intonation (*kāku*)— that should be known as "speech from the speaker" (*vaktrokti*), which is thus twofold.
Alliteration (anuprāsa), which consists in the similarity of phonemes, is twofold according to its occurrence in *cheka* or *vṛtti*.
The former involves multiple [sounds] once, while the latter involves even a single [sound] more than once.
That which is expressed by letters suggestive of sweetness is called *upanāgarikā*;
that which reveals *ojas* (vigour) is *paruṣā*, while others are *komalā* (soft).
For some, these styles (rīti), headed by Vaidarbhī, are considered [separate],
while the Lāṭānuprāsa is merely verbal, differing only in its intended meaning (tātparya).

It [the suffix] occurs after words, or even after a single word, whether in a compound or otherwise; it occurs after a noun, both when there is a compound and when there is not. Thus, it is considered to be fivefold.
When there is a meaning, that repetition of phonemes distinct from the meaning—occurring in the feet [of a verse] or their parts—is *yamaka*; it attains manifoldness.

When words, though distinct due to a difference in their expressed meanings, touch upon simultaneous utterance and thus coalesce, that is *śleṣa* (paranomasia); it is eightfold, based on syllables and other factors.

Since there is no difference [in the letters themselves], the difference [of the figure] would have to belong to the *prakṛti* and so forth as the ninth [element]. That is marvelous, wherein the letters become the cause of forms such as the sword and the like! (MK 85)
Furthermore, when appearing as a single entity, there is the appearance of words with distinct forms;
thus, this [relation] between word and meaning is like the singleness of the object for the word.
Similarity based on common properties is *upamā* (simile); it is divided into *pūrṇā* (complete) and *luptā* (elliptical), the former being the first.
It may be *śrautī* (verbal) or *ārthī* (conceptual), and likewise occur in a sentence (*vākya*), a compound (*samāsa*), or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
Similarly, when the common property (*dharma*) is omitted, the simile is no longer based on a *taddhita* suffix;
rather, it resides in a sentence (*vākya-gā*) or a compound (*samāsa-gā*) when the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is not explicitly mentioned.
When the verbal prefix (*vādi*) is elided, that [suffix] occurs in a compound, in *kyac* with the object or locus as the base, and in *kyaṅ*;
when both the object and the agent are elided, it occurs in *ṇamul*, in a *kvip* formation, and in a compound.
The elision of both the object of comparison (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is seen in both compound and sentence forms;
it occurs in *kyac* when the initial [syllable] and the object of comparison are omitted, and it is found in compounds where all three [elements] are elided.

When both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison belong to the same single thing within a single sentence, it is *ananvaya* (non-connection). When these two are reversed, it is *upameyopamā* (comparison of the compared).
Next, *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy) is the imagining of the subject at hand as being identical to another;
while *sasaṃdeha* (doubtful simile) consists of a state of uncertainty when the distinction [between the two] is either stated or not stated.

That is *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), which is the non-difference between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, when the [similarity] is expressed through a compound and is based on direct assertion (*śrauta*). When [the similarity] is superimposed [through implication], it is [a different type].
That [metaphor] in which both the literal and the implied meanings reside in a single part is "partial" (ekadeśavivartin).
This [type] is "with limbs" (sāṅga), while the "pure" (niraṅga) is as previously described; the "garland" (mālā) is likewise as before.
When the superimposition of one thing serves as the means for the certain superimposition of another, that is *paramparita* (transferred) metaphor;
it occurs when the expressive word is either *śliṣṭa* (homonymous) or possesses distinct meanings (*bhedabhāj*).
When one thing being under discussion is negated in order to establish another, that is *apahnuti* (concealment).
*Śleṣa* (paronomasia) occurs when there is a multiplicity of meanings within a single sentence.
Samāsokti is the expression of another [meaning] through words that are punned with qualifiers;
Nidarśanā is the non-existent connection between things which brings about the conception of a simile.
The statement of the concomitance of its own respective causes through the action itself is one [form of Aprastutapraśaṃsā];
that same Aprastutapraśaṃsā which has as its basis something already under discussion is another.

When the effect, the cause, the general, or the particular is under discussion, there are five types [of indirect expression]: the statement of something other than that, and likewise [the statement of] the equal for the equal.
Swallowing up [the literal sense] while determining the primary subject through another;
the identity of the subject with something else; and the conceptualization [of identity] upon the expression of "if" (yadyartha)—these are [other types of metaphorical identification].

When there is a reversal of the sequence between cause and effect, that should be understood as *atiśayokti* (hyperbole); however, when it serves as a point of comparison for every object (*prativastu*), it is *prativastūpamā* (parallelism).
Where a single common feature resides in two statements, that is the example; furthermore, for all of these, it is a reflection.

The single occurrence of a property belonging to both the relevant and the irrelevant subjects across many actions is called *dīpaka* (the illuminator). This refers to the case where a single grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is associated with multiple verbs.
The first is the Garland-Lamp (mālādīpaka), and then that which brings about subsequent qualities;
furthermore, the simultaneous application of a property to fixed entities is Equal Pairing (tulyayogitā).

When similarity has been presented in three ways— by means of the cause, by what is not stated, and by the triad [of the other two]— that very thing is the "distinction" (vyatireka) of another based on that comparison.
Likewise, when the word and its meaning are both suggestive and possess double entendre, that [type of *śleṣa*] is eighteenfold.
A negation of what is intended to be said, made with the desire to express a specific distinction, is [the figure of speech known as *apahnuti*]. (MK 10.6)
That objection (ākṣepa), whose subject matter has been stated or will be stated, is considered to be of two kinds.
Even when there is a negation of an action, the manifestation of its result is "Vibhāvanā" (the marvelous).
Viśeṣokti (peculiar cause) is the non-statement of the effect despite the presence of all its constituent causes;
Yathāsaṃkhya (correspondence) is the sequential coordination of successive items with successive items.
Whether it be a general rule or a particular instance, that which is supported by another—
either through similarity or otherwise— is *arthāntaranyāsa*.
That is contradiction (*virodha*), which is speech that treats as contradictory even what is not contradictory.
A genus (*jāti*) would be contradictory with four [other] genera and so forth, and with three qualities (*guṇa*).
Action [is expressed] by both [nouns], while substance [is expressed] by substance alone; thus there are ten [types of compounds].
As for *svabhāvokti*, it is the description of the form of its own action, such as that of a child and so forth.
*Vyājastuti* (feigned praise) is censure appearing as praise, or praise appearing as censure; its nature is otherwise [than what is expressed].
*Sahokti* (concomitant expression) occurs when, by the force of the sense of "together," a single word denotes two things.
Vinokti is that [figure of speech] where one thing is described as being non-existent without another; Parivṛtti is the exchange of objects, whether equal or unequal.
When past and future entities are rendered as if they were directly perceived, that is the *bhāvika* figure of speech;
it consists of a poetic reason (*kāvyaliṅga*) expressed through the meaning of a sentence or a word.

Paryāyokta (periphrasis) is speech that expresses [the intended meaning] without the relationship of signifier and signified; Udātta is the excellence of a subject matter and the characterization of great beings.

When there is a single cause for the accomplishment of something, and another [cause] also performs that same function, this is "conjunction" (samuccaya); however, that other [type of conjunction] consists of qualities and actions occurring simultaneously.
One [type of] formulation consists of [stating the reason] sequentially for multiple [instances], while another is otherwise;
that which is called inference is the statement of the probandum and the probans.
Parikara (the "enriched" figure) is an utterance using significant epithets;
Vyājokti (the "artful expression") is the concealment of the true nature of a thing that has been revealed through a pretext.
Whatever is stated— whether asked or unasked—
that serves to exclude something else, that is traditionally known as *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
If each subsequent [member] were the cause of each preceding meaning, then there would be a "garland of causes"; however, [this occurs] through their mutual interaction with the action.
Where the inference of a question is made from the mere hearing of a subsequent statement regarding the production of two entities, or where [that production] already exists; ||| MKpr-K_121 ||
When a response that was previously considered impossible occurs repeatedly, that is a true answer;
for even a subtle point, once discerned from some source, is made manifest to another.
Whereby it is described as subtle through some property, there would be a progressive excellence; that which reaches the ultimate limit is the essence (*sāra*).

When two properties that stand in a cause-and-effect relationship appear simultaneously despite being situated in entirely different locations, that is the figure of speech known as *asaṃgati* (incongruity).
Concentration is a task easily accomplished through the application of other causes,
provided that a suitable union [of conditions] is possible somewhere by virtue of their fitness.
In some cases, due to extreme disparity, no connection can be established;
for there is neither the attainment of the fruit of action by the agent, nor indeed any misfortune that might arise.
When the qualities and actions of the effect are respectively contradicted by the qualities and actions of the cause, this is considered the "unequal" (viṣama) [incongruous] type of incongruity.
When the two— the supported and the support— are respectively greater than the large and the larger,
then even if they are small in size, the support would still be greater than the supported.
When one who is unable to retaliate employs contempt as a countermeasure, that [contempt] serves to praise the very object of the attack; this is called *pratyanīka* (the "counter-attack").
When an object is concealed by another object of similar appearance—
whether that [concealer] be innate or adventitious— that is known as *mīlita* (the hidden).
Where an object is either established or excluded, each subsequent one being more excellent than the preceding by way of qualification, that is the two-fold *ekāvalī* (single-string ornament).
Just as there is recollection of an object upon seeing something similar to it according to prior experience,
so too is memory an error when there is a perception of something else that resembles it.
The reversal (*pratīpa*) consists in the subversion of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*),
or else the imagining of that very [standard] as the object of comparison (*upameya*), based on its disparagement.
When the subject at hand is joined with something else through the desire to express equality of qualities,
such that they are bound in identity, that is known as *sāmānya* (commonality).
Without a well-established substratum, there can be no persistence of that which is supported;
[otherwise] a single self would have simultaneous existence in multiple locations.

The threefold distinction is traditionally taught as follows: performing a different task while one is unable to perform a particular thing, and likewise, performing that very same task [in a different manner].

When a thing, by virtue of conjunction with something of exceedingly brilliant quality, abandons its own quality and assumes the quality of that other thing, it is called *tadguṇa* (the quality of that).
If it does not conform to that form, then it would lack those qualities;
just as when something has been established by one person in a certain way, another person establishes it otherwise.
In the same way, that which would be established [as such] is a contradiction; this is the traditional teaching (smṛti).
Their conjunction is desired when they exist here in distinction from one another.

But when [figures] that do not admit of rest within themselves possess the relationship of principal and subordinate, that is *saṃkara* (commixture). Furthermore, when there is uncertainty due to the absence of both a supporting reason (*nyāya*) and a subverting objection (*doṣa*) in favor of one [figure], that is *sandeha* (doubt).
It is evident that two poetic ornaments, consisting of word and meaning, are established together in a single subject; therefore, it is proclaimed to be threefold in form.
Although some of these faults may occur according to their respective applications, they are included within those already mentioned; therefore, they have not been explained separately.
Thus ends the series of verses belonging to the Kāvyaprakāśa.
